text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens abruptly with «This is the book of the generations of Adam» — a heading formula (Hebrew *toledot*) that recurs throughout the book to mark new sections. «Book» renders *sefer*, a written record or document; «record» or «account» would also be defensible, but «book» keeps the concrete sense of the Hebrew and the weight of a formal heading. The phrase *beyom bero* literally reads «in the day when God created», but *beyom* followed by an infinitive is a common Hebrew idiom simply meaning «when»; rendering it «When God created» keeps the natural rhythm without importing a twenty-four-hour reference. The same word *adam* occurs twice in the verse: first as the personal name Adam in the heading, then as the collective «man/humankind» as the object of creation. The translation lets the two senses stand side by side, mirroring the Hebrew, rather than smoothing them into one. «Likeness» renders *demut*, a term of resemblance, and «he made him» keeps the singular pronoun of the Hebrew, which then opens out into the plural «them» in the next verse.

*Toledot* derives from the root *yalad*, «to bear, beget», and denotes both descendants and the story that unfolds from an ancestor — hence its use as a structural heading. The interplay of *adam* (human being, mankind) with *adamah* (ground, soil) established earlier in the book still echoes here: the name is drawn from the dust from which the creature was formed. Note also the pairing of *bara* («create», used in Hebrew only of divine activity) and *asah* («make», a general verb of fashioning) within a single verse — a deliberate stylistic variation rather than two different acts. *Demut* («likeness») is a noun of resemblance from the root *damah*, «to be like»; it complements *tselem* («image») used in the first creation account.

The verse deliberately recalls the creation account: humanity bears the divine likeness. By restating this after the accounts of disobedience and the first murder, the text affirms that the likeness of God is not forfeited by human sin — a point taken up later in the book when the shedding of human blood is prohibited on precisely this ground. Interpreters have long debated what the likeness consists of: rationality and moral capacity, the capacity for relationship and covenant, or a representative, royal function as God's steward on earth. That the likeness is immediately followed by Adam's begetting «in his own likeness» (verse 3) has been read as suggesting that the image is transmitted to every generation.

Genealogies of this kind served in the ancient Near East to legitimate claims, organize memory and structure long spans of time; comparable king lists from Mesopotamia record rulers before and after a great flood, some with extraordinarily long reigns. The reference to a written «book» reflects a culture in which ancestral records were kept and cited as authoritative. Placing all humanity in a single documented line, however, is distinctive: it grounds every people in one ancestor made in God's likeness rather than tracing only a royal or priestly house.

The Greek tradition and some other ancient witnesses read «in the image of God he made him», substituting the word used in the first creation account for the Hebrew «likeness», apparently harmonizing the two passages. The Hebrew tradition's «likeness» is retained here as the more likely original. The Greek tradition also names the man «Adam» explicitly in this verse. In the Hebrew manuscripts a scribal marker closes the unit at the end of the following verse.

This verse begins the section of the Torah read as the second portion of the annual cycle in synagogue practice, and its affirmation that humanity is made in the divine likeness has long been cited in prayers and blessings concerning the dignity of human life, including funeral and burial liturgies.

text: Male and female he created them; he blessed them, and he named them Man on the day they were created.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew name given to the pair is 'adam, the same word rendered 'man' in verse 1. Since the verse says God named *them* — both male and female — with a plural pronoun, the word is functioning as a collective term for humanity rather than as a personal name; alternatives such as 'Humankind,' 'Humanity,' or simply 'Adam' are all defensible. Capitalized 'Man' is used here to preserve the naming act and to keep the verbal link with verse 1 and with 'Adam' in verse 3, where the same Hebrew word finally settles into a personal name. The closing phrase 'on the day they were created' renders a Hebrew idiom (be-yom + infinitive) that most often means simply 'when'; it is kept in its literal form here because it mirrors the identical construction in verse 1 and gives the sentence a rounded, memorable cadence for reading aloud.

'Male and female' translates zakar u-neqevah, terms drawn from biology rather than from social roles: neqevah is related to a root meaning 'to bore, pierce,' and zakar is used of the male of both humans and animals. The verb 'created' (bara') is used in the Hebrew Bible with God alone as subject, and it occurs three times in verses 1–2, framing the whole statement. 'They were created' is a niphal (passive) infinitive with a pronominal suffix, hibbare'am — a passive that quietly keeps God as the agent. The word 'adam also puns on 'adamah, 'ground, soil,' a wordplay made explicit elsewhere in the creation narrative.

This verse deliberately restates the creation account: male and female together, both blessed, both bearing the divine likeness, and both included under the single name 'Man.' The naming is significant — in this literature to name is to define and to claim, and here God names not an individual but the human pair as one. Read alongside verse 1, the passage grounds the unity and equal dignity of the sexes in creation itself, and the blessing recalls the mandate to be fruitful and multiply, which the genealogy that follows begins to trace out generation by generation.

Verses 1–2 form the heading of a genealogy structured like the long ancestral lists known from the ancient Near East, including Mesopotamian king lists with their extraordinary lifespans. Such lists served to anchor a people's identity in a remembered past and to bridge the gap between origins and present time. Placing the blessing of humanity at the head of the list frames the coming generations not as mere record-keeping but as the working out of that blessing.

The Hebrew text closes this verse with a scribal paragraph marker (setumah), indicating a break before the genealogy proper begins in verse 3. Ancient translations agree substantially with the Hebrew here; the Greek tradition renders the name as 'Adam,' treating it as a proper noun rather than a collective term, which reflects the same ambiguity present in the Hebrew.

versions.text: Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man on the day they were created.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, the chain of two consecutive "and" connectives slightly blurs the three parallel Hebrew clauses (created / blessed / named). Replacing the first "and" with a semicolon and repeating the pronoun before "named" gives the sentence a clearer three-beat cadence while keeping every element of the Hebrew intact.

text: When Adam had lived a hundred and thirty years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth.

versions.text: When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, numerals are better spelled out so the reader speaks them naturally without mentally converting digits; 'a hundred and thirty years' also gives the line a smoother spoken rhythm. The rest of the verse accurately renders 'in his likeness, after his image' and reads well aloud.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "and Adam lived thirty and a hundred years and he fathered"; English renders this with a temporal clause, "When Adam had lived a hundred and thirty years," which keeps the sentence moving in one breath for reading aloud. The verb wayyoled ("he fathered, begot") has no stated object, so "a son" is supplied from the sense; the older "begot" has been replaced with "fathered" for clarity. The number is spelled out here because the phrase falls inside a flowing clause, where digits would interrupt the rhythm.

The paired phrase bidmuto kətsalmo, "in his likeness, after his image," deliberately echoes 1:26–27, but with the two nouns and their prepositions reversed (there: bətsalmenu kidmutenu, "in our image, after our likeness"). Such crossing of terms is a common Hebrew way of tying two passages together while avoiding flat repetition. The name Shet (Seth) plays on the verb shit/shat, "to set, place, appoint" — compare 4:25, where Eve says God has "appointed" her another offspring in place of Abel.

By repeating the vocabulary of the creation account, the verse affirms that the divine image is not lost after the fall but is transmitted from parent to child; Adam's son bears Adam's likeness precisely as Adam bore God's. Interpreters differ on whether the image is thereby passed on intact, or passed on defaced — a question that has carried weight in debates about original sin and human dignity. Note also that here Adam does the naming, whereas in 4:25 the naming of Seth is attributed to Eve; the two accounts complement rather than contradict, since naming could be shared.

The Greek tradition gives Adam's age at Seth's birth as 230 years rather than 130, while reducing his remaining years from 800 to 700 so that the total of 930 (v. 5) is preserved. The Samaritan tradition agrees with the Hebrew here. This pattern of adding a century to the age at fathering recurs through the chapter and reflects competing chronological schemes rather than mere copying errors.

Genealogies of ten ancestors with extraordinarily long lifespans were a known way of organizing primeval history in the ancient Near East; Mesopotamian king lists assign their earliest rulers reigns of many thousands of years. Against that background the figures here, large as they are, are strikingly modest, and they diminish steadily as the narrative moves toward the flood and beyond.

text: After Adam fathered Seth, he lived eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Seth was born, Adam lived 800 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verses spell out numbers ("a hundred and thirty years"), so the digit form "800" breaks consistency and reads awkwardly aloud; spelled-out "eight hundred" suits oral reading. Also, the Hebrew keeps Adam as the subject ("after he fathered Seth"), matching the active phrasing of the previous verse rather than shifting to a passive "Seth was born."

versions.text: After he fathered Seth, Adam lived eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The current wording puts the pronoun "he" before its antecedent "Adam," which is momentarily confusing when heard aloud (a listener may wonder who "he" is). Naming Adam first in the opening clause and using "he" afterward keeps the same active phrasing and Hebrew word order sense while flowing more naturally for oral reading.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally reads, "And the days of Adam after he fathered Seth were eight hundred years." The rendering here recasts the noun-phrase ("the days of Adam ... were") as a verbal clause, "he lived eight hundred years," which reads more naturally aloud and matches the rhythm of the surrounding genealogy. The word "other" before "sons and daughters" is not in the Hebrew but is implied by the sequence: Seth has already been named, so the additional children are further offspring. The final clause is literally "and he fathered sons and daughters"; "he had" is used here because the verb covers the whole family, daughters included.

The phrase 'the days of X' (yemei) is a standard Hebrew idiom for a person's lifespan, used again in the next verse ('all the days of Adam'). The verb holid, a causative (hiphil) form of the root y-l-d ('to bear, bring forth'), is the term used throughout this chapter for a father's role in begetting; the same root in other stems describes a mother giving birth. The plural pair banim u-vanot ('sons and daughters') is a merism for offspring generally, indicating a large and unspecified number.

The genealogy follows a fixed formula for each generation: age at the birth of the named heir, years lived afterward, the fathering of other sons and daughters, total years, and death. This verse supplies the second and third elements. The mention of unnamed sons and daughters signals that the line traced here is selective, not exhaustive; the narrative follows one chosen thread from Adam to Noah while acknowledging humanity's wider increase, in keeping with the command to be fruitful and multiply.

Genealogies of this shape, with long-lived ancestors before a great flood, have parallels in Mesopotamian king lists, though those assign reigns of tens of thousands of years. The biblical figures are strikingly more modest by comparison. Ancient versions differ on the numbers in this chapter: the Greek and Samaritan traditions preserve alternative figures for several patriarchs, reflecting different chronological systems in antiquity, though the eight hundred years given here for Adam is stable across the main witnesses.

text: In all, Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Adam lived 930 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verse spells the number out ("eight hundred years"), so the numeral "930" is inconsistent and less suited to oral reading, where spelled-out numbers carry the rhythm of the genealogy more naturally.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "And all the days of Adam that he lived were nine hundred years and thirty years, and he died." The rendering "In all, Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years" compresses the wordy Hebrew summary formula into a single natural English clause, keeping the summarizing force of "all the days" in the phrase "In all." A more literal alternative, "So all the days that Adam lived were 930 years," is heavier on the tongue and less suited to reading aloud. The closing "and then he died" adds "then" to mark the sequence that Hebrew signals simply by the verb form; the bare "and he died" is equally possible. The total is spelled out in words here, rather than as digits, because the long round number carries a weight and cadence in speech that numerals lose.

Hebrew counts by repeating the noun with each element of the number: "nine hundred year and thirty year" (tesha' me'ot shanah ushloshim shanah). This is ordinary idiom, not emphasis, and English properly joins them into one figure. The phrase kol-yemei, "all the days of," uses "days" for a whole lifetime, a standard Hebrew way of speaking of a life span. The added relative clause asher-chai, "which he lived," is redundant in English but rounds off the formula in Hebrew. The verse ends with the scribal marker samekh, indicating a small paragraph break after each ancestor's notice.

"And he died" becomes the tolling refrain of this chapter, repeated for every name in the line except Enoch. Set against the sentence spoken in the garden, that on the day of eating he would surely die, and against the word that man returns to dust, the notice records the working out of that judgment even across a life of nearly a thousand years. Interpreters have read the immense life spans variously: as literal history of an earlier vigor of humanity, as a schematic or symbolic use of numbers, or as a deliberate counterpoint to the vastly longer reigns claimed in neighboring traditions. Whatever the reading, the point of the refrain is the same: length of days does not overcome death.

Ancient Mesopotamian king lists likewise assign enormous life spans and reigns to figures before the flood, some running to tens of thousands of years, after which the figures drop sharply. The biblical numbers, large as they are, are far more modest, and they too shrink dramatically after the flood. Genealogies of this kind functioned in the ancient world not only as record but as a way of ordering time and legitimating a line of descent.

The major ancient witnesses agree that Adam's total was 930 years, though they distribute it differently: the traditional Hebrew text and the Samaritan Pentateuch give 130 years before Seth and 800 after, while the Greek tradition gives 230 and 700. The differing splits, which recur throughout the chapter, reflect competing chronological systems for the age of the world rather than accidental copying errors.

text: When Seth had lived a hundred and five years, he fathered Enosh.

versions.text: When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, numbers are best spelled out rather than given as digits; the previous verse already uses words ("nine hundred and thirty years"), so spelling out keeps the rhythm and style consistent across the genealogy.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally counts "five years and a hundred years," placing the smaller number first, as is common in these genealogies. English idiom reverses the order, so the line reads "a hundred and five years." The verb rendered "fathered" is a causative form meaning "caused to be born, begot"; older renderings say "begat," while some prefer "became the father of." The Hebrew simply strings two clauses together ("Seth lived a hundred and five years, and he fathered Enosh"), but the temporal wording "When Seth had lived..." carries the same sense and keeps the sentence moving smoothly when read aloud.

The verse opens with the compressed form way-ḥî ("and he lived"), the same formula that governs the whole chapter and gives it its chant-like regularity: X lived so many years and fathered Y; X lived so many more years and had sons and daughters; all the days of X were so many years, and he died. The name Enosh (ʾĕnôsh) is one of the ordinary Hebrew words for "man, human being," often with an overtone of frailty or mortality — a fitting name in a chapter whose refrain is "and he died." It stands as a near-synonym of ʾādām, so that the first three names in the line, Adam, Seth ("granted, appointed"), and Enosh, quietly repeat the theme of humanity given and humanity mortal.

The genealogy deliberately follows Seth rather than Cain, tracing the line through which God's purpose continues after Abel's death. Enosh's birth was already noted earlier, where it is linked to people beginning to call on the name of the LORD, so this line carries the beginning of worship as well as the beginning of a family tree. Interpreters differ over whether the long lifespans are to be read literally, as symbolic or honorific figures, or as reflecting an ancient way of expressing dignity and the gradual diminishing of human vitality after Eden; in every reading the repeated "and he died" underscores the outworking of mortality.

The ancient witnesses disagree over the chronology of this line. The traditional Hebrew text gives Seth 105 years before Enosh's birth; the Greek tradition gives 205, with a correspondingly shorter figure for the years afterward, so that the total lifespan stays the same; the Samaritan tradition largely agrees with the Hebrew here. Such systematic differences run through the whole chapter and appear to reflect competing schemes for dating the flood rather than accidental copying errors.

Linear genealogies of this kind were a recognized literary form in the ancient Near East, used to anchor the present in the distant past and to legitimate a people's place in the world. Mesopotamian king lists likewise assign enormous reigns to rulers before a great flood — figures far larger than those here — and then much shorter spans afterward. Against that background these chapters present a restrained and orderly account of human origins in which ordinary fathers and sons, not divinized kings, carry the story forward.

text: After Seth fathered Enosh, he lived eight hundred and seven years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Enosh was born, Seth lived 807 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two adjustments: (1) Numerals ('807') break the rhythm of oral reading and are inconsistent with the spelled-out numbers in the surrounding verses ('a hundred and five years'); spelling out keeps the genealogy's cadence uniform. (2) The Hebrew has an active construction, 'after he fathered Enosh,' which matches the active verb used in verse 6 ('he fathered Enosh'); the passive 'After Enosh was born' unnecessarily shifts the subject away from Seth.

versions.text: After he fathered Enosh, Seth lived eight hundred and seven years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The current wording places the pronoun 'he' before its antecedent 'Seth,' which is awkward when read aloud, since a listener momentarily lacks a referent. Naming Seth first and using the pronoun afterward follows normal English order, keeps the active construction of the Hebrew, and flows smoothly in the genealogy's cadence.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally, "And Seth lived after his fathering of Enosh seven years and eight hundred years." Two adjustments serve English ears. First, the temporal clause is turned into a leading "After..." phrase, which is how English naturally frames such a sequence. Second, Hebrew customarily names the smaller number first ("seven years and eight hundred years"); English reverses this to "eight hundred and seven years." The word "other" before "sons and daughters" is not in the Hebrew, which says simply "and he fathered sons and daughters"; it is added because Enosh has just been named, and English idiom expects the distinction. The figures are spelled out in words here to keep the line reading smoothly aloud, while the summary total in the next verse is given as a numeral so the round sum lands clearly.

The verb rendered "fathered" is the causative (hiphil) form of the root yalad, "to bear, give birth"; used of a man it means "to beget, become father of." The phrase 'aharei holido is an infinitive construct with a pronominal suffix — "after his begetting" — a compact Hebrew construction with no smooth English equivalent, hence the finite clause "After Seth fathered Enosh." The chapter follows a fixed formula for each patriarch: years before the named son, years afterward, "and he fathered sons and daughters," and the total followed by "and he died." The repetition is deliberate and rhythmic, functioning almost like a refrain.

The ancient versions preserve differing figures throughout this genealogy. Where the Hebrew tradition gives Seth 105 years before Enosh and 807 afterward, the old Greek tradition reads 205 and 707; the Samaritan tradition agrees with the Hebrew here. All three arrive at the same total of 912 years, so the variation is systematic rather than accidental — the versions appear to have reworked the internal figures while preserving the lifespans, probably to adjust the overall chronology from creation to the flood.

The unnamed "sons and daughters" matter more than they may seem. They show that the genealogy is selective, tracing one line through humanity rather than recording every descendant, and they quietly account for the wider population presupposed by later chapters. The great lifespans have been read in several ways: as literal reports of a vitality gradually lost after the flood, as honorific or schematic figures in the manner of other ancient records, or as a narrative device showing the blessing of "be fruitful and multiply" still at work even under the shadow of the sentence "you shall surely die." Life is long, but the refrain of the chapter still ends each entry with death.

text: In all, Seth lived nine hundred and twelve years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Seth lived 912 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers read better spelled out, and this also matches the preceding verse's 'eight hundred and seven years.' Mixing numerals ('912') with written-out numbers in adjacent verses breaks the rhythm and consistency of the genealogy's repeating pattern.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "and all the days of Seth were twelve years and nine hundred years, and he died." Two adjustments serve the ear: the idiom "all the days of X were..." is rendered with the compact opening "In all, Seth lived...", and the Hebrew habit of naming the smaller figure before the larger is reversed to the English order "nine hundred and twelve." The closing "and then he died" adds "then" to mark the sequence for a listener; the Hebrew has only the bare verb form "and he died," which some render simply "and he died." The total is spelled out in words rather than digits so that the long summary line keeps its measured, chant-like cadence when read aloud.

"Days" (yamim) in the phrase kol-yemei stands for a whole lifespan, not for calendar days; the same idiom appears throughout the genealogy. Hebrew counts the years with the noun repeated after each numeral ("twelve years and nine hundred years"), a formulaic style that gives the list its rhythm but is not reproducible in idiomatic English. The final verb wayyamot ("and he died") is a single terse word, deliberately abrupt after the great number.

A paragraph marker (setumah) stands at the end of the verse in the Masoretic tradition, closing each generation as a small unit. The Samaritan tradition also gives Seth a total of 912 years, and the Greek tradition reaches the same total by a different route, assigning 205 years before Enosh and 707 afterward rather than 105 and 807. The lifespans of the individual patriarchs vary considerably among these traditions, yet Seth's sum agrees.

The refrain "and he died" closes every entry in this chapter except that of Enoch, quietly underscoring the sentence pronounced in the garden: however long the years, death has the last word. Readers have long noticed how the repetition builds pressure until Enoch's exception breaks it, and how the extraordinary lifespans are presented without comment or amazement, as simple record.

Ancient Mesopotamian king lists likewise assign enormous reigns to figures before the flood, though on a far larger scale, using tens of thousands of years. The biblical figures are modest by comparison and are structured around fatherhood rather than kingship, tracing a line of descent rather than a succession of thrones.

text: When Enosh had lived ninety years, he fathered Kenan.

versions.text: When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers should be spelled out rather than given as digits; the surrounding verse (v. 8, "nine hundred and twelve years") already spells them out, so "90" is inconsistent and reads awkwardly aloud.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "And Enosh lived ninety years, and he fathered Kenan." The rendering "When Enosh had lived ninety years" turns the first clause into a time frame, which is how the sentence functions: the ninety years are not the sum of his life but the point at which the next name in the line appears. The verb translated "fathered" is a causative form that means "caused to be born, begot"; it does not necessarily mean Kenan was the firstborn or the only son born by then, only that he is the son who carries the line forward. Some renderings prefer "became the father of" for clarity; "fathered" was chosen here for its compactness and steady rhythm, since this formula recurs many times in the chapter and needs to read smoothly aloud.

The name Enosh (ʾĕnôsh) is itself an ordinary Hebrew word for "man, mortal, humankind," often carrying overtones of frailty and mortality — a poignant name in a chapter whose refrain is "and he died." The name Kenan (qênān) is close in sound to Cain (qayin) and may be connected to the root q-n-h, "to acquire, beget," or to a word for a metalworker or spear. The chapter is built on a rigid formula — X lived N years and fathered Y; after fathering Y, X lived M years and had sons and daughters; all the days of X were T years, and he died — and the repetition is deliberate, a slow drumbeat that carries the reader from Adam to Noah.

The ancient numbers in this genealogy differ across the textual traditions. The received Hebrew text gives Enosh ninety years before Kenan's birth and 815 afterward; the Greek tradition reads 190 years before and 715 after; the Samaritan tradition agrees with the Hebrew here. In every case the lifetime total comes to 905 years, so the traditions differ over when the son was born rather than over how long the father lived. Similar patterns of a hundred-year difference run through the whole chapter, suggesting deliberate systems of reckoning rather than random copying errors.

Long lifespans in genealogies of primeval ancestors are a feature shared with other ancient Near Eastern king lists, though those lists assign vastly greater spans — tens of thousands of years — to their earliest rulers. Against that background the biblical figures are strikingly modest and human in scale. Ten generations are traced from Adam to Noah, matching the ten from Noah to Abraham, a symmetry that suggests the list is shaped for structure and memory as much as for arithmetic.

Enosh stands third in the line of Seth, the line through which the promise passes after Cain's descendants are set aside. Readers have long noted that this genealogy is the tally of death — each name ends with "and he died" — and yet each name also ends with a birth, so that the chain of mortality is also a chain of continuance. Enosh appears again in later Scripture as an ancestor in the line leading to Israel and, in the Gospel genealogy, in the line leading to Jesus.

text: After Enosh fathered Kenan, he lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Kenan was born, Enosh lived 815 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for accuracy and oral flow: (1) the Hebrew is active ("after he fathered Kenan"), keeping Enosh as the subject throughout, rather than the passive "After Kenan was born"; (2) since this text is optimized for oral reading, numbers are better spelled out, which also matches the spelled-out "ninety years" in the preceding verse.

versions.text: After he fathered Kenan, Enosh lived eight hundred fifteen years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements for oral flow: (1) naming Enosh in the opening clause avoids a pronoun ('he') that precedes its referent, which can momentarily confuse a listener; (2) adding 'and' in 'eight hundred and fifteen' reads more naturally aloud.

footnotes.text: Hebrew states the numbers in the reverse order of English idiom: "fifteen years and eight hundred years." The translation combines them into the single natural figure "eight hundred and fifteen years" for smooth reading aloud. The word "other" before "sons and daughters" is not in the Hebrew, which reads simply "and he fathered sons and daughters"; it is added because Kenan has just been named, and English implies the additional children were beyond him. The verb rendered "fathered" (a causative form of the verb "to bear") is used consistently throughout the chapter so the repeating rhythm of the genealogy can be heard.

The phrase "after Enosh fathered Kenan" translates an infinitive construct with a possessive suffix, literally "after his begetting of Kenan" — a compact Hebrew construction with no exact English equivalent. Note also the wordplay running through the chapter: the verb wayeḥi ("he lived") opens each entry and the verb wayyamot ("and he died") closes it, so life and death frame every name. The name Enosh itself is an ordinary Hebrew noun for "man, mortal," a quiet reminder of human frailty inside a list of extraordinary lifespans.

The ancient Greek tradition raises the age at which Enosh fathered Kenan to 190 and lowers the remaining years to 715, preserving the same total of 905. This pattern of adding a century before the birth and subtracting a century after it recurs for several patriarchs in this chapter, apparently to stretch the chronology from creation to the flood. The Samaritan tradition offers yet another set of numbers for some patriarchs. The figures given here follow the received Hebrew text.

Each entry follows a fixed formula: age at the birth of the named son, years lived afterward, mention of further sons and daughters, total years, and death. Comparable lists from Mesopotamia assign vastly longer reigns to rulers before the great flood, so the pattern of ten long-lived ancestors before a deluge belongs to a shared ancient way of telling the earliest history. The mention of unnamed sons and daughters reflects a genealogical convention that traces only the single line of interest while acknowledging a wider family.

The repeated note that each man "had other sons and daughters" shows the blessing to be fruitful and multiply taking effect despite the sentence of death pronounced in the garden. Life continues to be passed on, and with it the likeness of God spoken of at the head of this chapter; yet the closing refrain of death in the following verse keeps the reader mindful that the long years do not overcome mortality.

text: In all, Enosh lived nine hundred and five years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Enosh lived 905 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verse spells out numbers in words ("eight hundred and fifteen years"), while this verse uses digits. For a text optimized for oral reading, spelled-out numerals read more naturally and keep the rhythm of the genealogy consistent.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "and all the days of Enosh were nine hundred years and five years, and he died." "In all, Enosh lived..." renders the idiom "all the days of X were..." in a way that reads smoothly aloud while keeping its summarizing function: this is the total lifespan, the sum of the 90 years before Kenan's birth (v. 9) and the 815 after (v. 10). Alternatives such as "So all the days of Enosh were..." or "Enosh lived a total of..." are equally defensible; the chosen wording avoids beginning the sentence with a heavy "And all the days." The Hebrew lists the smaller number first ("five years and nine hundred years"); English convention reverses this to "nine hundred and five." The added "then" in "and then he died" makes the sequence audible without adding information, since the Hebrew verb form (wayyāmōt) already carries simple narrative succession.

The phrase kol-yəmê, "all the days of," is the standard Hebrew way of speaking of a person's whole lifetime; "days" stands for the span of a life rather than a count of calendar days. Note also that the noun šānâ ("year") appears twice, once with each number, and shifts between plural (šānîm with "five") and singular (šānâ with "nine hundred") — a normal feature of Hebrew number syntax, not a change in meaning. The Masoretic text closes the verse with the letter ס (setumah), a scribal paragraph marker that separates each patriarch's entry in the genealogy, giving the chapter its measured, list-like cadence.

Each entry in this genealogy ends with the same three words in Hebrew, "and he died," a refrain that tolls through the chapter. Read aloud, it presses home the outworking of the sentence pronounced in the garden. The refrain is broken only for Enoch (v. 24), whose omission is therefore all the more striking, and it sets the stage for the hope of a life not ended by death.

Extraordinarily long lifespans for figures of the earliest ages are also found in Mesopotamian traditions, such as the Sumerian King List, where pre-flood rulers reign for tens of thousands of years. Against that background the biblical figures are notably restrained, and they diminish steadily after the flood. Whether the numbers are meant as plain chronology, as symbolic or schematic values, or as a deliberate counterpoint to neighboring traditions has been debated since antiquity.

The ancient textual traditions differ over how the years before and after Kenan's birth are divided — the Samaritan tradition gives 90 and 815, while the Greek tradition gives 190 and 715 — yet all agree on the total of 905 years recorded here. The internal figures in verses 9-10 were adjusted in those traditions in ways that preserve this summary number.

text: When Kenan had lived seventy years, he fathered Mahalalel.

versions.text: When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers should be spelled out rather than given as digits; the surrounding verses use written-out numbers ('nine hundred and five years'), so 'seventy' keeps the rhythm and style consistent.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew is built of two simple clauses joined by "and": "And Kenan lived seventy years, and he fathered Mahalalel." Rendering the first clause as a temporal clause — "When Kenan had lived seventy years" — keeps the sense (the seventy years are his age at the birth, not the sum of his life) and gives the line the forward-leaning rhythm needed for reading aloud. The verb rendered "he fathered" is a causative form that can mean either "begot" or, more loosely, "became the ancestor of"; the traditional "begot" and the plainer "had a son" are equally possible. "Seventy" is spelled out here rather than given as a figure, matching the way the shorter, more chantable numbers are handled elsewhere in this chapter.

The name Kenan (Hebrew Qenan) is formally close to Qayin, "Cain," and to the root meaning "acquire, beget" or possibly "forge, smith"; its exact sense is uncertain. Mahalalel (Mahalal'el) is transparent: "praise of God" or "God is praise," from a noun for praise joined to the divine element El. It is the first name in Adam's line to contain El, and the second element of the genealogy's naming pattern is thus explicitly God-centred. The object marker before the name is the ordinary Hebrew sign of a definite direct object and has no separate meaning in English.

The ancient Greek tradition gives Kenan 170 years at the birth of Mahalalel and 740 afterwards, preserving the same total lifespan of 910 years found in the Hebrew and Samaritan traditions. Such systematic differences of one hundred years run through the whole chapter in that version and reflect a reworking of the chronological scheme rather than a variant in the name or the narrative itself.

Each link in this genealogy is stated in the same three beats: age at fathering, years remaining, death. The repetition is deliberate: it carries the blessing "be fruitful and multiply" forward through the generations while the closing "and he died" sounds the verdict pronounced in the garden. Kenan's entry adds nothing individual — no deed, no word — which is precisely the point: life continues, unremarkable and mortal, until the line reaches Enoch, who does not die.

Genealogies of this kind, listing ten generations from a first ancestor, have parallels in the king lists of ancient Mesopotamia, where the rulers before the flood are likewise credited with enormous spans of years. In such lists the names function as public memory and as a claim to legitimate descent; the numbers belong to a conventional way of measuring the distance to the beginning of things rather than to record-keeping in a modern sense.

text: After Kenan fathered Mahalalel, he lived eight hundred and forty years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Mahalalel was born, Kenan lived 840 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two refinements: (1) The Hebrew has the active construction "after he fathered Mahalalel," matching the active verb in verse 12; the passive "After Mahalalel was born" shifts the subject away from Kenan. (2) For a text optimized for oral reading, spelling out "eight hundred and forty" flows better than the numeral and keeps the genealogy's cadence consistent.

versions.text: After he fathered Mahalalel, Kenan lived eight hundred and forty years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The current wording puts the pronoun "he" before its antecedent "Kenan," which is awkward when read aloud. Naming Kenan first and then using the pronoun follows the natural flow of English and keeps the genealogy's cadence clear for a listener.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew begins "And Kenan lived, after he fathered Mahalalel, eight hundred and forty years." The translation moves the time clause to the front — "After he fathered Mahalalel, Kenan lived..." — because in English the interrupted sentence stalls the voice, while the front-loaded clause keeps the chapter's chant-like rhythm intact for reading aloud. The Hebrew states the number as "forty years and eight hundred years"; English idiom reverses this to "eight hundred and forty years." The number is spelled out here, whereas the larger total in the next verse is given in figures, so that the ear (and eye) can rest on the summing-up. The word "other" in "other sons and daughters" is not in the Hebrew, which reads simply "sons and daughters"; it is supplied because English otherwise leaves the impression that Mahalalel is not counted among them.

The phrase 'aḥarê hôlîdô is an infinitive construct with a pronominal suffix — literally "after his fathering of" — a compact Hebrew construction that English must unfold into a full clause ("after he fathered"). The verb yālad in its causative (hiphil) form means "to beget, become father of"; in the simple form it means "to give birth," so the same root covers both parents. The paired expression bānîm ûbānôt, "sons and daughters," is a merism: two poles standing for the whole of one's offspring, and thus for a full, blessed household.

The ancient manuscript traditions differ over the figures in this genealogy while agreeing on the totals. The Hebrew tradition behind this translation gives seventy years before Mahalalel's birth and eight hundred and forty after; the Samaritan tradition agrees; the ancient Greek tradition reads one hundred and seventy before and seven hundred and forty after. All three arrive at a lifespan of nine hundred and ten years, which suggests the variation arose in the transmission of the intermediate figures rather than in the summary total.

Each link in this chapter follows a fixed fourfold pattern: age at the birth of the named son, years lived afterward, the birth of further sons and daughters, and the total followed by "and he died." Such formulaic ancestor lists were a recognized way of ordering the deep past in the ancient Near East, where long-lived antediluvian figures also appear in Mesopotamian king lists, though with vastly larger spans. Here the repeated cadence functions almost as a metronome, marking the generations from Adam to Noah.

The unnamed "sons and daughters" quietly show that the blessing of fruitfulness given in creation is being carried out, even as the refrain "and he died" in the following verse shows the sentence of mortality taking effect. The line traced by name is thus not the whole of humanity but the thread through which the promise moves forward.

text: In all, Kenan lived nine hundred and ten years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Kenan lived 910 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: The preceding verse spells out the number in words ("eight hundred and forty years"), so the numeral "910" here is inconsistent and less suited to oral reading. Spelling out the number preserves the rhythm of the genealogical refrain and lets a reader voice it naturally.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "and all the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years, and he died." The rendering "In all, Kenan lived..." turns the Hebrew noun phrase into a verb, which reads more naturally aloud and keeps the summarizing force of "all the days." Alternatives such as "So all the days of Kenan came to nine hundred and ten years" preserve the idiom more literally but sound stiffer in oral reading. Hebrew lists the numeral as "ten years and nine hundred years"; English convention reverses this to "nine hundred and ten." The full figure is spelled out rather than written as digits so that the closing cadence of the lifespan formula matches the other totals in the chapter. The added "then" in "and then he died" renders the simple Hebrew conjunction, marking the finality of the sequence without adding new content.

The formula opens with a plural verb agreeing with the plural subject "all the days" (kol-yemei), an idiom in which "days" stands for a whole lifetime rather than individual days. Note the shift between the plural "years" with the small number (eser shanim, "ten years") and the singular "year" with the hundreds (tesha me'ot shanah), a normal feature of Hebrew counting. The verse closes with the terse two-syllable wayyamot, "and he died" — the same clipped word that ends each notice in this chapter, giving the genealogy its drumbeat rhythm.

The relentless refrain "and he died" runs through the chapter as the working out of the sentence pronounced in the garden: however long life is extended, it ends. Its regularity makes the single exception all the more striking, when Enoch "was not, for God took him" (5:24). Some readers see in these long lifespans a memory of humanity nearer its origin and less worn by mortality; others read the numbers as literary and symbolic, shaped to structure ten generations from Adam to Noah. Either way, the theological point of the chapter is the same: life is a gift passed on through generations, and death is the boundary of every human story except where God intervenes.

Extraordinarily long lifespans for figures before a great flood are a feature of other ancient Near Eastern traditions as well; Mesopotamian king lists assign reigns of tens of thousands of years to rulers before the deluge. Against that background the figures in this chapter, all under a thousand years, are strikingly modest, and they diminish steadily after the flood. Kenan's name reappears in later genealogical recitations of Israel's ancestry, showing how these lists were preserved and reused as a framework of memory.

The Hebrew text closes the verse with a scribal paragraph marker (a "closed" section break), indicating a small pause before the next patriarch is introduced. The chief ancient witnesses — the traditional Hebrew text, the Samaritan tradition, and the early Greek translation — all agree on Kenan's total of 910 years, even though they differ over the figures for several other patriarchs in this chapter.

text: When Mahalalel had lived sixty-five years, he fathered Jared.

versions.text: When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers are better spelled out; this also matches the surrounding style (verse 14 reads "nine hundred and ten years"). Spelled-out numerals give the reader a smoother rhythm and avoid a visual stumble in the genealogical cadence.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally reads "And Mahalalel lived five years and sixty years, and he fathered Jared." The rendering "When Mahalalel had lived sixty-five years" turns the Hebrew coordinate clause into a temporal clause, which is how English naturally expresses the sense: the years are the age reached at the time of the birth, not a period of life that ended then. The number is written out in words here to fit the rhythm of the sentence, while the larger figure in the next verse is given as digits for ease of reading aloud. "Fathered" renders a causative verb meaning "to beget, bring forth"; alternatives are "became the father of" or "had a son," but the shorter verb keeps the repeated formula of the chapter crisp when spoken.

Mahalalel (mahalal'el) is built from a root meaning "to praise" plus El, "God" — thus "praise of God" or "God is praised." Jared (yered/yared) is most naturally connected with the verb yarad, "to go down, descend," giving a sense like "descent" or "one who goes down." The Hebrew here shows the pausal form yared at the end of the verse, while verse 16 has the ordinary form yered; this is a normal vowel shift caused by the accent at a pause, not a different name.

The Hebrew tradition and the Samaritan Pentateuch both give sixty-five years for Mahalalel's age at Jared's birth; the Greek tradition reads one hundred sixty-five, part of a consistent pattern in which the Greek adds one hundred years to the pre-fatherhood figures of several patriarchs while subtracting the same amount from the years lived afterward, so that the total lifespan stays the same. The translation follows the Hebrew text.

This is the fifth link in the chain of ten generations from Adam to Noah. Each entry follows a fixed pattern — age at the birth of the named son, years lived afterward, other children, total years, death — so that the repetition itself carries the message: life continues, generation after generation, yet each notice ends in death. Only Enoch, two names later, breaks the pattern. Some readers have heard significance in the names themselves, with "praise of God" followed by "descent," though the text draws no such conclusion.

Ancient Near Eastern king lists and genealogies also assign very long spans to figures of the earliest ages, though the numbers there are vastly larger — reigns of tens of thousands of years. Against that background these figures are strikingly restrained, and the genealogy functions less as a modern chronology than as an ordered account of humanity's earliest generations.

text: After Jared was born, Mahalalel lived eight hundred and thirty years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Jared was born, Mahalalel lived 830 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, numerals are better spelled out, and this also matches the spelled-out form used in the surrounding verses ("sixty-five years"). Otherwise the rendering reads smoothly and accurately reflects the Hebrew.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally, "And Mahalalel lived after his fathering of Jared thirty years and eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters." The translation turns the Hebrew infinitive phrase ("after his fathering of Jared") into a short clause, "After Jared was born," which reads more naturally aloud than a literal rendering; the sense is unchanged, since the Hebrew still has Mahalalel as the father. The Hebrew habit of naming the smaller number first ("thirty and eight hundred") is reversed to the English order "eight hundred and thirty," and the figure is spelled out rather than written in digits so that a reader can move through it without stumbling. The word "other" before "sons and daughters" is not in the Hebrew but is implied: Jared has just been named, so those who follow are additional children. "Had" is used for the Hebrew verb "fathered" here for smoother rhythm; the causative form itself simply means "begot, became father of."

The name of the son appears as יָרֶד (with a long vowel) in the previous verse, where it stands at the end of the clause in pausal position, and as יֶרֶד here in ordinary context; these are the same name, not two different people. The verb וַיְחִי ("and he lived") opens both verses and functions as the fixed frame of the genealogy. The formula אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ, "after his fathering," uses a causative infinitive with a possessive suffix — a compact construction with no neat English equivalent. The paired phrase בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת, "sons and daughters," is a merism meaning simply "children."

The genealogy of Genesis 5 is built from seven repeated elements: name, age at fathering, name of son, remaining years, further children, total years, and the closing "and he died." This verse supplies elements four and five. Ancient Near Eastern king lists and genealogies likewise used long life spans and rigid formulas; here the pattern serves both to link Adam to Noah and to mark the steady march of generations.

Ancient Greek witnesses to Genesis give Mahalalel 165 years before the birth of Jared and 730 afterward, while the Hebrew has 65 and 830 — a systematic shift of a hundred years found throughout this chapter in that tradition. Notably, all traditions agree on the total of 895 years given in the next verse. The Samaritan tradition agrees with the Hebrew here.

The mention of further sons and daughters shows that the line traced in this chapter is selective, not exhaustive: it follows one chosen thread toward Noah while acknowledging that humanity multiplied widely, as commanded in Genesis 1:28. The blessing to be fruitful continues to be fulfilled even in a chapter whose refrain is "and he died."

text: In all, Mahalalel lived eight hundred and ninety-five years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Mahalalel lived 895 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: The number is written as a numeral here, while the immediately preceding verse spells the number out ("eight hundred and thirty years"). For a text optimized for oral reading, spelled-out numbers read more naturally and keep the genealogy's rhythm consistent.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "and all the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died." The rendering "In all, Mahalalel lived..." keeps the sense of a closing total while avoiding the heavier phrase "all the days of," which reads awkwardly aloud after the same formula has appeared in each preceding generation. Hebrew states the numbers in the order "five and ninety years and eight hundred years"; English convention reverses this to "eight hundred and ninety-five." The added "and then he died" reflects the simple Hebrew connective while marking the finality that the formula carries at the end of each life; some renderings keep the bare "and he died." Note also that spelled-out numerals are used here for the summary totals, while the shorter fathering-age figures nearby appear as digits, a rhythm choice for reading aloud.

The phrase kol-yemei, "all the days of," is a Hebrew idiom for the full span of a lifetime; "days" stands for the whole of life rather than a count of individual days. The verb wayyihyu ("and they were") governs the plural "days," so the sentence is literally a summing-up rather than a statement about living. The name Mahalalel (mahalal'el) is built from a root meaning "to praise" plus El, "God," hence "praise of God" or "God is praised." The clipped closing verb wayyamot, "and he died," consists of a single word in Hebrew — abrupt and final.

The traditional Hebrew text closes this verse with the scribal marker samek, indicating a small paragraph break (setumah) at the end of each generation's entry. These markers are part of the received scribal layout rather than the wording of the text, and they show that the genealogy was read as a series of distinct, self-contained units. The ancient Greek tradition distributes Mahalalel's years differently (165 years before fathering and 730 afterward), yet arrives at the same lifetime total of 895; the Samaritan tradition likewise agrees on the total. Where the early witnesses diverge in this chapter, it is usually in the split between the two figures rather than in the sum.

The refrain "and he died," repeated for every generation in this chapter, functions as a drumbeat confirming the sentence pronounced in the garden: mortality now governs the human line. Its relentless repetition is what makes the single exception a few verses later — Enoch, of whom it is not said — stand out so sharply. Long lifespans in this list have been read in several ways: as literal reckoning, as reflecting an ancient tradition of a diminishing vitality after creation, or as a stylized scheme in which the numbers carry symbolic weight. In any reading, the point of the chapter is not longevity but the unbroken transmission of life and blessing from Adam toward Noah, despite death's claim on each generation.

Genealogies with formulaic lifespan totals are known from the wider ancient Near East, where king lists likewise assign enormous reigns to figures before a great flood, with far shorter figures afterward. Compared with those lists, whose pre-flood rulers are credited with tens of thousands of years, the spans here are strikingly modest. The naming of sons and daughters without personal names, and the focus on a single line, reflects the ancient practice of tracing descent through one representative heir rather than recording a complete family census.

text: When Jared had lived one hundred and sixty-two years, he fathered Enoch.

versions.text: When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verses spell out numbers in words ("eight hundred and ninety-five years"), which suits a text optimized for oral reading; digits like "162" break the visual and rhythmic consistency for a reader speaking aloud. Spelling the number out matches the established pattern of the genealogy.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "two and sixty year and a hundred year," listing the smaller unit first and repeating the word "year" with each figure. English idiom requires the reverse order and a single plural noun, hence "one hundred and sixty-two years." The opening verb is literally "And Jared lived a hundred sixty-two years and fathered Enoch"; rendering the first clause as a temporal phrase ("When Jared had lived...") keeps the sense that this was his age at the time, not the sum of his life, and it lets the sentence move in one breath when read aloud. The verb translated "fathered" is a causative form meaning "caused to be born, begot"; older wording is "begat," and some render it "became the father of." As elsewhere in this chapter, the named son need not be the firstborn — he is simply the one who carries the line forward.

The name Jared (Hebrew Yered) is built on the root y-r-d, "to go down, descend," and is naturally heard as "descent" or "he goes down." Enoch (Ḥanokh) comes from a root meaning "to dedicate, initiate, train up," the same root behind the word for "dedication." The chapter's rhythm is deliberately formulaic — lived, fathered, lived, fathered sons and daughters, and he died — so that any break in the pattern (as with Enoch two entries later) stands out sharply to the ear.

The ancient versions differ on the pre-fatherhood ages in this chapter. The Greek tradition agrees with the Hebrew here in giving Jared 162 years, while the Samaritan Pentateuch reads 62, with a correspondingly shorter total lifespan. Such variations run through the whole chapter and appear to reflect competing chronological systems for the span from creation to the flood rather than simple copying errors.

Jared's significance in the narrative lies chiefly in his son: Enoch is the seventh from Adam, the one man in this list of whom it is not said "and he died." The relentless death-refrain of the chapter, sounding the verdict of the garden, is interrupted precisely at Enoch — a hint, within a genealogy, that walking with God opens a way through mortality.

In later Jewish tradition Jared's name was linked to the "descent" of the watchers in the days of Jared, a story elaborated in the Enochic literature, where heavenly beings come down upon a mountain and corrupt humanity. That literature also made Enoch a visionary and scribe of heavenly secrets, and it circulated widely in the centuries around the turn of the era, which is why Enoch is invoked in some New Testament writings.

text: Jared lived eight hundred years after he fathered Enoch, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Enoch was born, Jared lived 800 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for consistency and oral reading: (1) the surrounding verses spell out numbers in words ("one hundred and sixty-two years"), so "800" should be "eight hundred" for a reader's ease; (2) the Hebrew has the active "after he fathered Enoch," matching the active verb used in verse 18, rather than the passive "after Enoch was born." Naming Jared in the main clause keeps the subject clear.

versions.text: After he fathered Enoch, Jared lived eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Placing "Jared" before the pronoun avoids a forward-referencing "he," which can momentarily confuse a listener at the start of a read-aloud sentence. It also mirrors the Hebrew word order, where Jared is named first and the "after he fathered Enoch" clause follows.

text: In all, Jared lived nine hundred and sixty-two years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Jared lived 962 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: Since the text is optimized for oral reading, spelling out the number gives a smoother rhythm and matches the spelled-out figure in the previous verse ("eight hundred years"), keeping the genealogy consistent for a reader aloud.

text: When Enoch had lived sixty-five years, he fathered Methuselah.

versions.text: When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, numbers should be spelled out rather than given as digits; this also matches the surrounding verses, which write numbers as words (e.g., 'nine hundred and sixty-two years').

text: After he fathered Methuselah, Enoch walked with God three hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Methuselah was born, Enoch walked with God 300 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for oral reading: (1) numerals like "300" should be spelled out ("three hundred") since the text is meant to be read aloud, and this also matches the spelled-out style needed elsewhere in the genealogy; (2) the Hebrew has an active construction ("after his fathering of Methuselah"), so keeping the active voice matches the original and preserves continuity with the preceding verse's "he fathered Methuselah."

text: In all, Enoch lived three hundred sixty-five years.

versions.text: In all, Enoch lived 365 years.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers are better spelled out so the reader's eye and voice flow without pausing to convert digits; it also matches the wording of the surrounding genealogy ('three hundred years' in v. 22).

text: Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God took him.
When Methuselah had lived one hundred eighty-seven years, he fathered Lamech.

versions.text: When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech.
versions.explanation: For a text optimized for oral reading, numbers should be spelled out, as was already done in verses 22 and 23 ('three hundred years,' 'three hundred sixty-five years'). Mixing digits with spelled-out numbers within the same genealogy breaks the rhythm for the reader.

text: After he fathered Lamech, Methuselah lived 782 years, and he had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Lamech was born, Methuselah lived 782 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew "אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־לֶמֶךְ" is active ("after he fathered Lamech"), matching the wording of verse 25 ("he fathered Lamech"). Keeping the active voice preserves the repeated genealogical formula, which aids oral reading rhythm, rather than shifting to the passive "After Lamech was born."

text: In all, Methuselah lived nine hundred sixty-nine years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Methuselah lived 969 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: Consistency with the spelled-out numbers in verses 22-23; digits interrupt the flow when the text is read aloud.

text: When Lamech had lived one hundred eighty-two years, he fathered a son.

versions.text: When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son.
versions.explanation: Spelling out the number keeps the genealogical formula uniform with verses 22-23 and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands, because of the ground that the LORD has cursed."

versions.text: He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands, caused by the ground the LORD has cursed."
versions.explanation: The participial phrase "caused by the ground" is slightly awkward for oral reading and reverses the logical direction of the Hebrew מִן ("because of / on account of"). "Because of the ground that the LORD has cursed" flows more naturally when read aloud and keeps the causal sense clear.

text: After Noah was born, Lamech lived 595 years and had other sons and daughters.

versions.text: After Noah was born, Lamech lived 595 years, and he had other sons and daughters.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses an active construction ("after he fathered Noah"), and the genealogy's repeated formula reads more smoothly aloud without the extra "and he" clause. Dropping the second subject pronoun and the comma tightens the rhythm and matches the pattern used elsewhere in the chapter, while "After Noah was born" is retained as a natural English rendering.

text: In all, Lamech lived seven hundred seventy-seven years, and then he died.

versions.text: In all, Lamech lived 777 years, and then he died.
versions.explanation: Spelling out the figure matches the style established in verses 22-23 and serves oral reading better than digits.

text: When Noah was 500 years old, he fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

versions.text: After Noah was 500 years old, he fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew simply states Noah's age alongside the birth of his sons; "After" adds a chronological nuance not present in the text and reads awkwardly aloud. "When" matches the pattern used for the other genealogical entries and flows better for oral reading.
